newsitem.title: Austria: Albania enforces emergency, south out of control.
newsitem.headline: Albania enforces emergency, south out of control.

text.p: Albanian troops enforced emergency rule on Tuesday in an effort to stamp out the violence that has sent the southern part of Europe's poorest country reeling out of control.
Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu defended the emergency measures, saying they had succeeded in pulling the mountainous state back from the brink of civil war.
But opposition parties told President Sali Berisha the way to stop further bloodshed was to agree to a new, broad-based government.

After weeks of protests sparked by the collapse of speculative investment schemes, officials issued orders to shoot armed rioters on sight, imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew and curbed press freedoms after parliament declared a state of emergency.

"With this ruling the risk of civil war has diminished hugely. If we had not taken it, do you know what would have happened? That today Tirana would have been attacked by the rebels," Shehu told Italy's leftist daily L'Unita.
He said the south was "completely out of control".
But the United States said it strongly regretted Albania's imposition of emergency as well as a vote by the Balkan country's parliament to re-elect President Sali Berisha.

"We strongly regret the measures taken by the parliament and government today to, in effect, introduce a state of emergency and to introduce censorship of the Albanian press," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
"We're very concerned that the state of emergency declared by the parliament today is being used to stifle legitimate free expression," Burns told a news briefing.
Burns sharply criticised the election of Berisha on Monday to a second five-year term.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, stressing the alliance was not a world policeman, ruled out military intervention and said diplomacy was the key to solving the crisis.
The European Union, meanwhile, was preparing to discuss the crisis on Thursday with Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo who is due to visit Albania on Friday.

In his interview, Foreign Minister Shehu told the Italian newspaper: "Up to now we have tried to act as prudently as possible to avoid armed clashes and bloodbaths. This line has not paid off and now the military operations start."
Asked whether this meant that the army would now attack the south, Shehu replied:
"Nothing of the sort. We will act calmly. It will probably take a few days to reinforce the law in Vlore. In the meantime, however, the rebels must hand over their weapons."
He said banks and libraries had been ransacked in the southern towns of Vlore and Sarande and that a navy ship had been seized by "rebels" in the south.
At least 12 people were reported killed at the weekend after crowds in several southern towns raided weapons depots and went on a rampage of burning and looting.
On Monday tanks were spotted in Gjirokaster and gunfire from automatic weapons was occasionally heard there on Monday, Greek diplomats and eyewitnesses said.
Italian television said a stray bullet killed a child in Vlore on Tuesday, but this could not be independently confirmed.

"Vlore is in chaos, waiting. The rebels, who have seized small military boats, today looted food stocks from the hospital, and there are reports that a girl of four has been killed by a stray bullet," the television correspondent said.
Witnesses said on Tuesday that southern Albanian villages, just across the Greek border, were at the mercy of armed gangs who killed a taxi driver, looted shops and set fire to warehouses.

"Carloads of armed gangs with automatic weapons and hand grenades roamed through the villages of Vryssera and Jorgucat throughout the night and early this morning," local resident Christo Otero told Reuters in Athens by telephone.
Also on Tuesday, the Italian Defence Ministry said an Albanian military plane had landed in southern Italy and that its two pilots had asked for political asylum.
In Tirana, Albania's main opposition Socialist party told President Berisha a new government was the way out of the crisis.
Pandeli Majko, one of three Socialist leaders at the talks, said the party had gained "no sense of compromise" from Berisha at the meeting, their first since the state of emergency was declared.
"We told Berisha we were ready for a wide political accord under which he would stop using the army...and we would agree to form a new broad-based government," Majko told Reuters.
"We are convinced it will be difficult to achieve this but we told Berisha it is no longer a matter of left or right but of protecting people and stopping further blood from being shed.
"We told him that if we reached a common political view then ordinary people who are now on the streets without knowing why would dissociate themselves from the disorder," he said.
Asked what was Berisha's response, Majko said the president had told the Socialists, successors to Albania's old communists, "not to try to take power by arms".
"We advised him that we would never want power through blood," Majko said.
Analysts, meanwhile, said Albania faced the economic abyss and it could take years for the impoverished country to recover.
"The immediate consequences could be very dire. In the short term, it could be complete chaos," Vladimir Gligorov, Albanian expert at the Vienna Instiutute for Comparative Studies, told Reuters.
The local currency, the lek, was falling, while both inflation and unemployment were rising. The average monthly wage was little more than $65.
Britain followed Washington on Tuesday in criticising President Berisha's government.
"Stability cannot be restored by force alone," Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said. "President Berisha must work with the opposition to restore faith in the democratic process."
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Tuesday he was "extremely concerned" about the situation as well as restrictions on foreign media there.

A ministry statement said Kinkel had asked the current chairman of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, to send an OSCE delegation to Albania as a matter of urgency.
U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan said he was disturbed by the current unrest and urged government restraint.
Responding to an international outcry over media restrictions, an Albanian justice ministry spokesman, Agim Neza, said the curbs did not apply to foreign news organisations.
"You are free to report," Neza told Reuters.
Western television broadcasts resumed from Albania on Tuesday, a senior official of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) said.
